Self-hosted Zcash infrastructure · one Docker image

Run your own Zcash stack. No landlord.

Zovereign restores a mainnet archive node and lightwalletd from published snapshots, wires them together over a private loopback RPC, and hands your wallet a gRPC endpoint on your own machine. One container. One volume. Nobody else’s server in the middle.

§ 01

Things you can stop doing.

Running Zcash wallet infrastructure used to mean a weekend of glue. Zovereign does the glue, and does it the same way every time.

  1. Renting an RPC endpoint from someone else and hoping it stays up and stays honest about tip height.Your wallet server talks to your node, over loopback, inside one container.
  2. Rebuilding years of chain history block by block before anything is useful.A published archive snapshot restores that history; the node only processes what came after.
  3. Hand-writing RPC credentials and wiring two daemons that must start in the right order.No credentials to manage. lightwalletd waits until Zakura is near tip, then starts.
  4. Restarting a 275 GB download because the Wi-Fi blinked.Range downloads resume from committed bytes, pinned to the same snapshot.
  5. Calling it “healthy” because a port is open.Healthy means lightwalletd just served a real compact block from your node.

§ 02

From two crates of history to a block in your wallet.

On first boot, Zovereign turns about 300 GB of compressed snapshots into a running node and wallet server. Every step is checked, resumable and boring in the best way. Here is the actual sequence.

  1. 01 · Pin

    Pick a snapshot and stick to it.

    The latest compatible mainnet archive is chosen from the Zakura manifest, and the latest lightwalletd cache from its own. Each choice is pinned to disk, so a restart finishes the same snapshot even if “latest” moves.

  2. 02 · Fetch

    Download in checked ranges.

    256 MiB HTTP ranges, parallel connections and retries. Offsets and sizes are verified and bytes commit in order to a .part file, so an interruption costs you minutes, not the whole download.

  3. 03 · Verify

    Hash every byte.

    The complete compressed archive must match its SHA-256 before anything is unpacked. A mismatch throws the archive away instead of handing your node a corrupt history.

  4. 04 · Stage

    Unpack somewhere safe first.

    Extraction goes into a staging directory. Only regular files under the expected paths are accepted: no traversal, links or special files. The validated result is renamed into place, never sprayed over existing data.

  5. 05 · Drop root

    Give up the keys to the building.

    The volume is locked against a second node, then bootstrap, Zakura and lightwalletd all run as UID/GID 10001. Nothing that talks to the network keeps root.

  6. 06 · Catch up

    Node first. Wait for the tip.

    Zakura starts in mainnet archive mode and must answer RPC within five blocks of its estimated network tip before anything else happens. It only has to process blocks newer than the snapshot.

  7. 07 · Serve

    Then the wallet server. Then proof.

    lightwalletd starts against loopback RPC with its compact-block cache already populated. Docker reports healthy only after it serves an actual block from one behind your node’s tip.

  8. 08 · Every boot after

    Skip steps 01–05 forever.

    A completed bootstrap is reused without contacting either snapshot publisher. From now on, startup is a node restart that catches up on whatever it missed, not a reinstall.

§ 03

Inside the box.

One process tree, two daemons, one volume, three ports, and a clear opinion about which of them the internet gets to see.

  1. 1

    Supervisor

    Tini handles PID 1 while a Python supervisor downloads, verifies, restores, drops privileges, and runs both daemons as a pair: if either exits, its peer is stopped and Docker restarts the whole stack.

  2. 2

    Zakura archive node

    Full mainnet history in archive mode, restored from a snapshot instead of rebuilt from the network, then kept current from peers.

  3. 3

    Private RPC

    Node RPC listens on 127.0.0.1:8232 inside the container. It is never published to the host. No credentials to generate, rotate or leak.

  4. 4

    lightwalletd

    Starts with a populated compact-block cache and catches up from your node. The health probe makes it serve a real block before Docker calls the stack healthy.

  5. 5

    One named volume

    zovereign-data holds both databases and any unfinished downloads. It outlives the container, so updates mean replace the box, keep the data.

  6. 6

    Peer port 8233

    The one port meant for the internet: the node’s connection to other Zcash peers.

  7. 7

    Wallet port 9067

    lightwalletd gRPC, bound to your host’s loopback by default. Serving another machine is a deliberate choice: an SSH tunnel, a private network, or your own TLS certificate.

§ 04

Why it’s worth the disk.

i.

You skip the slowest part on purpose.

An archive node’s history is the expensive bit. Zovereign downloads it as a verified snapshot instead of replaying it from the network, then lets your node do the live work. The win is not a magic number. It is not doing the historical rebuild at all.

ii.

The whole stack, not just a node.

A node without lightwalletd can’t serve a light wallet. lightwalletd without a node needs someone else’s RPC. You get both, started in the right order, configured against each other, and watched as one unit.

iii.

Failure is a planned state.

Downloads resume. Corrupt archives get rejected. Extraction errors clean up their own staging. An incompatible database is refused instead of silently replaced. Installed data is never overwritten by a bootstrap that doesn’t recognise it.

iv.

Private until you say otherwise.

RPC stays inside the container. Wallet gRPC is on host loopback. Daemons run unprivileged. Opening it to the world is something you do on purpose, with a tunnel or TLS, not something you discover in your logs.

We ran the full thing against real mainnet snapshots on a clean Linux amd64 VPS (12 CPU threads, 32 GiB RAM, 1 TB SSD). These are dated results from that run, not a live counter.

This was one run on a fast, well-connected host. It is not a benchmark and we haven’t measured a same-hardware from-scratch baseline. Your first install depends on bandwidth, disk and how far the chain has moved since the snapshot.

  • Reached the live tip and served an actual compact block through gRPC.
  • Removed compressed archives and range files after restore.
  • Restarted, reused both databases with no new downloads, and came back healthy.
  • Served a client on another machine over a private Tailscale-bound port.

§ 06

Bring a real machine.

This is an archive node, not a toy. First boot moves about 300 GB compressed (≈275 GB Zakura + ≈25 GB lightwalletd), then verifies and extracts it, so plan the disk accordingly.

On a fast SSD host with good bandwidth, expect the first end-to-end install to take roughly 2–3 hours. Slower links and disks take longer. Later starts reuse the data.

Recommended
CPU
4 cores
Memory
16 GiB
Storage
SSD
Data capacity
1 TB
  • Linux amd64 — tested platform.
  • Docker Desktop / WSL 2 — allocate these resources to Docker’s VM, not just the host.
  • Native ARM64 — not supported.
  • Apple Silicon — runs under amd64 emulation; a full mainnet restore has not passed validation there.

§ 07

Start it.

No registry login, separate RPC provider, Docker-in-Docker or RPC credentials. Pick one way to run it. Both create the same zovereign container and zovereign-data volume.

Published image · nothing to clone

shell
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 \
  --name zovereign --restart unless-stopped --stop-timeout 120 \
  --log-driver json-file --log-opt max-size=20m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  --mount type=volume,src=zovereign-data,dst=/data \
  -p 8233:8233 -p 127.0.0.1:9067:9067 \
  ghcr.io/zcashlabs/zovereign:latest
  • --mount …zovereign-data keeps databases and download progress across container replacement.
  • 127.0.0.1:9067 publishes wallet gRPC to your machine only.
  • --stop-timeout 120 gives both databases time to flush on stop.

From source · build locally with Compose

shell
git clone https://github.com/zcashlabs/zovereign.git
cd zovereign
docker compose up -d --build
  • Same defaults: bounded logs, two-minute shutdown grace, loopback gRPC, persistent volume.
  • Optional: copy .env.example to .env to change ports, download concurrency or disk reserve.
  • Pause with docker compose stop; resume with docker compose start.

Then · watch it work

logs
docker logs -f --tail=100 zovereign

Then · ask if it’s ready

health
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' zovereign

starting during bootstrap. healthy once the node is near tip and a real compact block came back.

Then · point a wallet at it

127.0.0.1:9067

Any wallet or gRPC client that supports a custom plaintext server. For other machines, use a trusted tunnel or configure TLS.

Keep the volume. Stop gracefully with docker stop -t 120 zovereign. Removing or replacing the container keeps zovereign-data; deleting the volume means downloading ~300 GB again.

§ 08

The fine print, in large print.

Snapshots are a shortcut, and shortcuts have a shape. Here it is, so nobody has to find it in a footnote.

What a SHA-256 check buys you

  • Proof the archive you got is the archive the manifest described, byte for byte.
  • Protection against truncated, corrupted or tampered-in-transit downloads.
  • Your own node and wallet server afterwards: no remote RPC backend in your wallet’s path.

What it doesn’t

  • Authentication. A publisher who can replace both the archive and its manifest can replace the checksum too.
  • From-genesis verification. Imported history is trusted to the snapshot publishers.
  • So: self-hosted, yes. “Trustless”, no. We’d rather you know.

§ 09

Questions people actually ask.

How long does the first start take?

Hours, not minutes. It has to download roughly 300 GB, hash all of it, extract it, then let Zakura catch up past the snapshot. On a fast SSD host with good bandwidth we estimate 2–3 hours end to end; our own development run took about 99 minutes including interruptions. Slower disks or links take longer, and we don’t promise a fixed time.

And every start after that?

Much shorter. A completed bootstrap is reused without contacting the snapshot publishers, so a restart is just the two daemons starting on existing databases and catching up on whatever happened while they were stopped.

What if my download gets interrupted?

Start the container again. Completed ranges persist in a .part file and the chosen snapshot is pinned, so it resumes the same archive rather than starting over, even if a newer snapshot has been published in the meantime.

Do I need a separate full node, RPC provider or credentials?

No. Zakura is bundled, its RPC listens on loopback inside the container, and lightwalletd connects to it there. There is no Docker socket, no registry login and no credentials file to manage.

Can my phone wallet use it from elsewhere?

Not by default, deliberately. gRPC binds to your host’s loopback. To serve another machine, use an SSH tunnel or a private network, or mount a certificate and key and set TLS_CERT / TLS_KEY. The deployment guide shows the exact command.

What happens if one of the daemons crashes?

They live and die as a pair. If either exits, the supervisor stops its peer gracefully and exits, and Docker’s restart policy brings the whole stack back on the same volume.

Will it run on my M-series Mac?

It runs under amd64 emulation, but a full mainnet restore under emulation has not passed validation, and native ARM64 isn’t supported. Linux amd64 is the tested platform. On any Docker Desktop, allocate the CPU, memory and disk to Docker’s VM.

How do I update without losing anything?

Pull the new image, stop with a 120-second grace period, remove the container, and run the same command again with the same zovereign-data volume. The databases stay put. Check release notes first: an incompatible database is refused, not silently replaced. Pin a sha-<commit> tag or digest when you want controlled upgrades.

Is this trustless?

No. Checksums protect integrity, not authenticity, and imported history depends on the snapshot publishers. What you do get is your own node and wallet server, with no third-party RPC in the path from here on. See the fine print.

Own the endpoint your wallet talks to.

One image. One volume. One command. The rest is your node’s business.
